utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik? Are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, we are ready and he will be the first of our expert witnesses. He will be testifying in open session. It is Mr. Stiepo Andrijic and we are quite ready. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as the witness is being brought in, or rather, I will examine the witness regarding certain facts which are very distressing for the Defence and this is not the first time. There are also some other distressing news which seem to be aimed at the obstruction of our defence but let us first hear the witness and then I will tell you what this is all about. I do not want to testify in advance because I've heard your warnings that I was testifying instead of the witness so I'd rather ask a few questions of this witness and then we can see what this is all about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you to listen to me carefully, I will give you some instructions so that we can work better. I know this is the first time for you here and it always takes time to get used to this environment. But professor, you can see the screen in front of you, and you can see this dot which is moving.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to be so kind as to, since we both speak the same language, and so as to allow our interpreters to interpret into two languages, as best they can, to therefore wait for this dot to stop, and then start your answer. You will see now how I've finished speaking. The dot has come to a stop and then you may start speaking.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: See, now it's stopped.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, will you please introduce yourself to the Court, give us your name, tell us where and when were you born, and then we shall briefly go through your career?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I am Stiepo Andrijic. I was born 58 years ago, and I will first say what I am doing now and then I'll go to the beginning, to the time of my birth. I'm a teacher, that is a regular professor at the faculty of economics of the University of Sarajevo, at the faculty of economics of the university in Split. I also had the postgraduate studies in insurance at the faculty -- at the university in Zagreb. I am the president of the Society of Economists, Benko Kortolic, in Mostar. And the society of actuaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. I completed elementary education in the place of my birth, then the secondary school in Kakanj, the high school of economics in Sarajevo, the faculty of economics in Sarajevo, post-graduate studies at the institute of economic sciences in Belgrade, which at that time was headed by professor Branko Horvat. I defended my doctoral thesis at the faculty of economics at Sarajevo in 1975. In professional organisations, I held the posts of the President of the society of economists of the city of Sarajevo. I am a member of the board for the economic sciences of the academy of sciences and arts of B and H. I taught the following subjects; macroeconomics, econometrics, international payments. I was the President of the commission for sciences and arts of the University of Sarajevo and a member of the editorial board of a number of scientific journals. Outside the university, I was the governor of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a member of the cabinet of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a minister without portfolio. I headed the privatisation study in the federation. I headed an expert team of the government of the federation for privatisation, which drafted 14 systemic laws, which have passed the whole procedure and have been adopted by the parliament. And my last office was president of the management board of the steering board of the privatisation agency in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe this suffices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, shall I address you as professor or academician, I don't know what you would rather?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: As you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then it will be easier for me to address you as professor from my students days. I got used to that. Professor, have you also been awarded for your scientific work --

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In 1989, the award of the city of Sarajevo for scientific results achieved in the quantitative economics and my work at the university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about international tributes?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I have the award for humane -- the Charter for Humaneness of the International -- I can't remember what it's called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The International Charter for Humaneness?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, before I ask you several questions, and before I turn you over to the Prosecutor, I'd like to ask you whether you talked with any journalists about your today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give your expert work to any journalist? I mean your expert analysis that you did for this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask Madam Registrar if she could request the usher to get us D1/389, please? I'm sorry, I'm sorry, we are about to produce it, because we intended to produce it and we put a number, so could the usher please help me to distribute it, to give it to Their Honours and the Prosecutor? Because we prepared it today only, of course we shall prepare three copies for Your Honours. I merely wished to first ask some questions of this witness about this and then during the break, we shall provide more copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could the usher put this document on the ELMO? And I believe that the Prosecutor needs one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's what I wanted to ask you because I have nothing on my desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have a copy for you, Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, why didn't you do it beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right and I apologise. I do apologise for not having done it earlier. We shall not be tendering this document. We produce it merely as information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So professor, are you familiar with the article that you can see there on the ELMO? Well, turn around and look at it. No, no, no, it's not that article. Could you then please put the English version on the ELMO and let the professor read the article?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could somebody else read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know, read it, just read the "Croatian Tender Legitimate."

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About a month ago, were you disturbed by this article because it says that you'd be prosecuted? Does it refer to your expertise on the whole and when did you read it poor the first time?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: It appeared about a month ago, and I can comments on this because it is very simple. This is very ugly. And when you say something is ugly in our language, you know what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no further questions with regard to this article. I don't wish to speak in front of the witness, I will wait for him to leave but I want to say that a month ago, in Dani which is a Sarajevo weekly, there appeared an article about the expert testimony of Mr. Andrijic, what and how he will be testifying. It is really curious how they came by his analysis but I do not want to tax the witness's patience with it right now. Professor, would you please be so kind as to tell us if you were a member of any party, if you -- after 1990?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, did you discharge any duty in the authorities of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna or the Croat Republic Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, tell me, in the authorities of the then Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which duties did you discharge, until when? When did you leave and why?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I was the governor of the national bank from the end of April, 1992, until the 5th of October, 1993. That means that I discharged the duties of the governor for about a year and a half. As for the latter part of your question, I was dismissed on the 5th of October, 1993. While I was in Washington, attending the regular annual assembly of the international monetary fund and the World Bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who dismissed you and why?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Well, it should have been the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but at that time there were only three members in the Presidency, and in 1992, they were elected in the regular elections for the Presidency. Needless to say, the signature is the -- that of the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us his name?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this lawful dismissal? Could Mr. Izetbegovic or those three members of the Presidency, did they act lawfully?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm an economist, I'm not a lawyer, and if there are only three members of the Presidency out of seven, then the conclusions, as to the legality should be taken by those who studied law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, when you attended regular assemblies of the IMF or some other international organisations, were you ever denied -- was your status ever questioned? Were you denied the right to represent Bosnia-Herzegovina there?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No. I performed those duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they -- and what about the Muslims, Bosniaks, who were in the presidency or in some other organisations that is bodies, did they try to deny you the right to do that?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, I performed my duty normally until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my last question, why were you dismissed?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I can only quote what the decision it for my dismissal says and it says that I did not perform my duties properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to tell us if that was true?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: How could it be true if I was attending the annual assembly as the governor, attending it ex officio with all the regular travel orders and everything else and participated in the work, in the -- in all the ways in which it was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question, professor, can you explain to Their Honours what were the powers of the governor of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Well, that is common knowledge. The governor of the national bank, or rather -- has powers or rather the national bank is empowered to conduct the monetary policy and beyond that, it has no other powers. It is an independent organisation and accountable only to the assembly, within the framework of the law, that is even the parliament cannot act outside the law. That would be the most important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I merely ask you, is it your signature on this expert analysis that you signed in March, that is on the 22nd of March, 2002? Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is your document and your expert opinion, is it?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, professor. I have no further questions. I have your expert analysis. That is your opinion. That is your testimony. And now I turn you over to colleagues, to our learned friends from the Prosecution who wanted to examine you because of whom you are here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Krsnik. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Poriouvaev:

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the usher to distribute the bundle of documents with our potential exhibits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I don't think that I will have too much questions for you but still I will have a few questions. My first question will be, have you ever been qualified as an expert in financial matters?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I have never been that, but in this case, I can be that, given all the elements that I have given you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by your biographical notes attached to your report, you had never practised as a bank functionary before you were appointed governor of the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any written works on the financial matters, in particular on the use of foreign currency in domestic monetary operations?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What written works of yours have been published? Do you remember them? Maybe you can give names, titles of some of your works, written works.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Those are papers from the area of the arbitration of foreign currency, the conversion of loans, and it is very hard for me to remember all of them, but I can supply them to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever testified as a financial expert in domestic courts?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, once in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you testified for the Defence or for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I believe I was invited to testify by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: It was some 20 years ago, ten years before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a criminal or a civil case?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: It was economic crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you just stated that you were appointed the governor of the national bank in April, 1992, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom were you appointed to this position?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was its duty and it also had the duty of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no parliament as such at the time to appoint you as the governor, as in the normal situation they do?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: The war had already begun and the parliament stopped functioning, and therefore the provisions of the constitution applicable to the war conditions had already started being applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you have your main office in 1992 and 1993, until you were dismissed from your position?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: In the building of the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, in Titova street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay in your main office throughout the wartime, I mean 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in my office all that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have deputies?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I had a vice governor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only one?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I had two vice-governors. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are always three members of such bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of all currency operations? I mean with foreign currency? You personally or one of your deputies?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I had one of my vice governors discharging the duties of a deputy with regard to foreign currency matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you present any annual report to the presidency? Instead of parliament? Since the parliament did not exist at the time?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we also -- the presidency considered all the documents which would normally be considered by the parliament. Those were the loan policy and reports on loans and the loan policy. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when did it take place, I mean the presentation of your report?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was in April, 1993, for the previous year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your report approved by the presidency?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they make any substantial remarks to you for the fulfilment of your duties as a governor of the bank? I mean at that point, after your annual report.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll return to this topic a little bit later. Now I would like to pass on to your report, because I've got some questions. Is it correct that Herzegovinian dinar was introduced as a national currency on the 15th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Can please my learned friend clarify? In our first bundle of documents we had Bosnia-Herzegovina and now the Prosecutor has used the word Herzegovinian dinar, so which dinar is he referring to Bosnian, Bosnian-Herzegovinian or just Herzegovinian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a slip of my tongue, I meant of course the Bosnia-Herzegovinian dinar, I'm sorry, I'm awfully sorry. So I wait for your response. Is it correct that it was introduced as a currency on the 15th of August? At least the decision provided for introduction of this currency as of the 15th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: It was introduced on the 15th of August, 1992, and it was used in those areas that were accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so before this, the Yugoslav dinar was the only lawful currency in Bosnia-Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Formally and legally it was but simply that dinar, effectively, did not exist any longer and all the accounting, all the books, were in Yugoslav dinars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Yugoslav dinar continued to exist as a currency for some period of time after a new currency had been introduced, right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, no. The new currency was introduced on the 15th of August. Until then, we used the Yugoslav dinar but we had cash problems, there was no cash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question, just from this set of questions, was it allowed to use any other currency but Yugoslav dinars before the 15th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: In conditions of war, all the money that is available is used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you, but was there any official decision endorsing the use of foreign currency in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I would kindly ask that the professor is taking time when giving his answers, and the Prosecutor may think that he has finished but obviously he needs time to finish his questions, so if we could allow the witness to take time and finish his answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a legitimate request. I myself thought that the witness has already finished his answer. Mr. Prosecutor, you might wait a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you answer my question. My question was about any official decision endorsing the use of foreign currency in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the new currency was introduced in August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Under the laws that were in effect at the time, and those laws had been taken over from the pre-war Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were some possibilities, some specific possibilities, to use foreign currency, only for cash payments under the laws prevailing at the time, had to be in local currency. However, all the parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina were encircled and there was no physical access to them. You know that the mint was in Belgrade and that the -- that cash could not reach Bosnia and Herzegovina from Belgrade, and that is why we used for cash payments only the cash that was to be found at the time in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the little that was in the vault of the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These quantities were insufficient for the functioning of the payment transactions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, let's go to point 6 of your conclusions. In point 6 of your conclusions you claim that all domestic banks in their operations were controlled by the national bank, right? Which period of time did you mean in your report?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: While I was the governor. I can talk only about the time while I was the governor and up to the time when I was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't ask you about another period of time. I ask you questions only relevant to you. Could you explain how did the national bank manage to regulate and supervise all the activities of the local bank once the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993 was very difficult and Sarajevo was actually isolated?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: As the central bank, we managed, and all the banks were correct and we had direct cooperation, during that period of time, ten new banks were incepted in Sarajevo, one in Mostar, and licence was given to some branch offices of the banks which were headquartered in Sarajevo and could not have contacts with the headquarters so we licensed them for independent operations, just temporarily of course, for as long as the war was on. This had to be done for the purpose of maintaining some sort of a banking system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive reports from the local banks on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: The notion of "regular" is very difficult to define under war circumstances, but we did have certain contacts, because at that time, we could not communicate by telephone with Sarajevo, only the satellite connections were on. We tried what we could, and whenever we could, through the office in Zagreb, because the BH government had its office in Zagreb, and that office helped the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, we would be correct to say that in the circumstances, you were working as a governor of the national bank, it was very difficult if possible at all, to control the local banks?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Not only do I think but I'm sure that we managed, given the circumstances, and all the banks complied with the decisions of the central bank, and I believe that this institution worked to a certain level which at the time was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible to check bank operations by any audit organisations?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Only based on their reports could we carry out control, and the direct control was in the areas that were accessible, either from Sarajevo or from the areas surrounding Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that control over the reports from the subordinate banks is an effective form of control?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: One can't say that it is as in peace time but everything was done to make the system as integral as possible and in conditions of war, I think that it functioned better than any other institution. Again, I'm speaking of the time when I was the governor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will I be correct if I state, for example, that your allegation about the effective control, is a little bit exaggeration? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that. Given the conditions that prevailed, I believe that all of the institutions, the contacts between business banks and the central bank, was good enough, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, as a governor of the national bank, I suggest that you were aware that some local authorities were adopting decisions, introducing foreign currency as means of payment in their territories, and they did it even before the 15th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a governor of the national bank, you were not aware of the use of foreign currency in some territories?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I believe that foreign currency was used in all free territories, not only do I think that but I claim that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were the local authorities authorised to issue such kind of acts?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: It is very hard to say, in legal terms, in formal terms, the answer is no, but in conditions of war, something had to be done to provide for people's survival. Even in Sarajevo, when there was no domestic cash, we used all the money that was available, but there were also barter agreements, even in the centre of Sarajevo, for a while, the monetary unit that was in use was a box of cigarettes, the box of the Drava cigarettes. Its value was about 6 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the non-cash operations?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about uncash operations, operations between the enterprises just payment by accounts.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that in the entire territory, there were no payment transactions, because the economy, the industry, didn't work, and the little that was produced was distributed and one cannot talk about payment transactions under such circumstances in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Sarajevo, for example, and another encircled areas, there were no -- there was no trade that would require non-cash transactions. Only the population was the segment that did have some cash from the pre-war times, regardless of the currency, and all the currencies available at the time were in use in -- among the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show to professor exhibits number 136.2 and 136.3. 136.2. That's a decision of the Crisis Staff of Kiseljak municipality; is that correct? Do you have this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to read this document to yourself.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have your local bank in Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: At that time, I believe there was no local bank. There was a branch office which was probably closed down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you see, this decision was issued on the 15th of June, 1992. Was it lawful?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you see -- can't you see?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: A moment, please. It's very hard for me to say whether it was lawful or not. Simply this was a war area, an encircled area, and such a decision obviously is not in compliance with the work of the central bank, but it is very hard to leave the people in an encircled area without any money whatsoever because at the time, the Yugoslav dinar was still in effect but they did not have the cash there and what I find more important is the second part of this decision, which says that any foreign currency can be used for payment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to Exhibit 136.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As you see, I waited to finish this document. It says as the source that it comes from the ICTY witness. Could the Prosecutor say whether it is the person who signed this document? Did he testify? Or who is truly the source of this document? Because all it says here is "ICTY witness."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor? I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, we got this document -- these two documents and another two documents, really from witness who testified in another case. If it is necessary, we can go into private session. Then I will inform in which case that the witness testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So professor, you claim that all these decisions were made just in favour of the local population, am I right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, no. That is not what I said. What I did say was that under the circumstances, one needed to ensure the sales, because in that area, one could not find cash. I mean Yugoslav dinar was not available there. So the only solution for this municipality, which is in encirclement and the only solution for it was to perhaps print some coupons which could then be used as legal tender, and you know that any paper money is nothing else but a coupon, a scrip. So this was the solution they devised and you can see that in this case, any currency, that is German mark and dollar and Austrian schilling could be used as a legal tender in an enclave which was under siege. This was a sensible solution and I do not think it was a political decision. It was a sensible decision to ensure some functioning of the economy, albeit minimal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: If I may, I'm sorry, may I add something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: In the area of Bihac, coupons were printed and they had the German mark design because they simply could not come by any money whatever. In Tuzla, the same thing was done. In Zenica, the same thing was done. We happened to be in Sarajevo, so that we had physical possibility to print these scrips, these coupons as money and it was different from the money that was used in the rest of the free territory. Of course it is not the same because this was done by the national bank, but in a manner of speaking, any -- every encircled part of Bosnia-Herzegovina had, in a way, powers to ensure some kind of sales, some kind of traffic, and that meant also that some kind of the local legal tender had to appear. These is a purely economic solution, helping not to waste money, to print more bank notes, if there were already some others, in addition to the Croatian dinar, all the world currencies were in use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the usher to show to the professor Exhibits P155.1 and 157.4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I don't claim that you were supposed to know about those two letters, but what I want to ask you, and I hope you will understand, that there were some grounds for some part of the population of Kiseljak municipality, some ethnic parts of the population, to be discontented with such kind of decisions. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, it seems to me that it's the time for the break or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we still have five minutes to go. If you want to finish this two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I've done with these two documents, now I will pass to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I need to say that in these documents, provided by the Prosecution, the source of them is once again ICTY witness. These documents are without dates. We do not know who these members are because there are only signatures, there are no names typed. Such a document, I can type such a document in ten minutes time, if need be. We do not know who are these people who signed it, members of -- they are members of what? It says members. It says "members, signatures," but no date. What body they belong to, where they -- are they members, who are they writing to? I mean, we just don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think just now, it's well that you raise this issue after using the documents. I believe that those questions will be answered after we use those two documents by the Prosecutor. And Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed with your questions and after that set of questions, you may answer the question put by the Defence counsel concerning of the origin of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I can give you a response just straight away. These documents were provided to us by the same witness who provided us with our first two documents, and they were admitted by us in one set of documents, and that's why they were used here. As for the admittance of the documents by this Trial Chamber, the Defence counsel may file his objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, but I also have a question. On the right corner of the B/C/S version there is a stamp. Within that stamp there are some dates on it. I just want to know whether this date is the date for this document or for the filing of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I suggest, Your Honour, that this is a note made by the investigator while he was receiving the documents from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed with your questions on those two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I have completed my questions with these two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents. I got a response from the witness. He agreed with me that there were some grounds for discontent of people in the areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. May we break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will break now. We will break until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, some explanations about these documents. I checked with the transcript and I'm afraid that I have misled you a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: If you take a look at the right, upper corner of the original document, I mean 155.1, you will see the stamp confirming that the document was received by the Kiseljak municipality people, which is 8 of July, 1992, the first one, and Exhibit 157.4, this same stamp in the right, upper corner, the document was received on the 13th of July, 1992, and in the left, bottom corner of the first document, you will see remarks made by the investigator. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, that is the point, and I waited for the Prosecutor to say that, and I'm asking you, on the 13th of July, 1992, the internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be called the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina municipality of Kiseljak, and that is what the stamp says. And that is why I started wondering what it was about, because at that time it was called only the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After Dayton, the word "republic" was dropped off, but in July, 1992, it was not the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we will deal with this issue when we are admitting those documents into evidence, and I thank you very much for the point you made. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, in your report, item E, you analyse in detail the financial policy of Sarajevo leadership, and you claim that they introduced deutschmarks as means of payment, right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the financial policy of Herceg-Bosna leadership, which was not isolated at all from the outside world? I don't see that you analysed it in your report. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: There was no need to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, were you aware that at some point, president of Herceg-Bosna community, Mate Boban, issued decrees introducing Croatian dinar as currency, which was stated in legal enactments?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that but I can comment on it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First much all, I would like you to take a look at one exhibit, and then maybe then maybe you will give some explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the professor to be shown Exhibit 183.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I mean, two decrees, first decree, decree on the implementation on the law on public law and order of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during war, or of the imminent threat of war. And the other one, also decree on the implementation of the law on the road traffic safety and so on again, in the territory of this community Herceg-Bosna. I would like to draw your attention to Article 3 of the first decree and to Article 2 of the second decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not know about the copy that the professor has, but we do not have Article 3 in Croatian. We only have one half of the first sentence in our copy. If you will have a look, this is the Croatian original. I don't know what you have, but Article 3 only has about two-thirds of the first sentence and nothing else. I do not know whether the professor has the full text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that the English version and the B/C/S version are not corresponding to each other, but I'm not quite sure. Maybe Mr. Prosecutor could shed some light on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have both articles, Article 3 of the first decree and Article 2 of the second decree, just on the same page, they are all on the same page in B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. I'm not quite convinced about the contents of those two articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: That's page 8 -- six, in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, Your Honour. I looked at the English translation and the English translation does not correspond to the Croatian original. Article 2 is the decree on the fines prescribed in case of violation of the public peace and order, and in English it is something completely different. Article 3, I can't see it, I see only two-thirds of that sentence. And the rest of the text I cannot see, so that this English version does not have anything to do with the Croatian original, and I'm quite sure that our accomplished interpreters can resolve it in no time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I suggest that the interpreters can help us, if we give them our English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. As for the Article 3, are you talking about the page 00860161?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I mean in English version, the last three digits are 782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: In the English version, Article 3 of the first decree and Article 2 of the second decree, also on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. How about the B/C/S version, on which page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: On B/C/S version, sorry, it's digit 162. The last three digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. I think that's where the confusion comes from. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no, there isn't any confusion. This is what it is all about. The pages that you have read, 782, and Croatian version 162, the English translation has nothing to do with the Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could ask the interpreters to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe -- I think that the booths have.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we also have faulty copies of the Croatian original, and on page 162 of the Croatian version. Booth speaking now, I think that the problem is with the photocopy. We are missing the part of the Article number 3 of the first decree, it's not photocopied. With the beginning of Article 2 in the decree on the enforcement of the road safety law but otherwise we do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On page 162, Article 3 I only have one sentence in my copy, I mean the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: But Article 2 is all right, it's complete? Article 2 of the second decree is complete?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is true, but could the interpreters help us and tell us if Article 2 on page 782 is identical with Article 2 on page 162 of the Croatian original? One can see it with the naked eye. Article 2 has --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two Articles 2 on the Croatian version. That is on page 162. There are two Articles 2. One is the decree on the enforcement on the public order, public peace and order of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is an Article 2 which is rather long and contains a number of figures, and there is another decree which is the enforcement of the road safety law, which has a different Article 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How about Article 3 on the same page? In Article 3, I only have one sentence. I think it's a problem of the copying.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have more than part of the sentence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is not the problem. The translation is completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: What is different? I don't see any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian original that I can see says, and if the interpreters can help us, "The fines are set and imposed in Croatian dinars," if you can see properly. And Article 3 of the English version says, "This decree shall enter into force on the day of its issue." That is the English translation of the Croatian original that I've just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I can't agree with the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 3, that is what I'm doing because Article 3 in Croatian, one can see only part of the sentence, is not what the English translation of Article 3 says. I'm saying that the translation of the Croatian original does not correspond. That is what we see Article 3 translated into English on page 782 and Article 3 in Croatian on page 162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid we have to ask the interpreters to translate Article 2 of that decree into English. We'll hear what the difference it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, which decree? Because there are two -- three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On the page 162, right column.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Article 2, therefore, in the decree on the enforcement of the road safety law on the roads of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Article 2 roads "the fines shall be set and pronounced in Croatian dinars in the same nominal values in which they are prescribed in the law indicated in Article 1 of this decree."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see no substantial difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: If you take a look at Article 3 it begins with the same sentence. If it is not complete, you will see the same sentence, about the monetary fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll take note of that and you may proceed, Mr. Prosecutor, with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, did you know about this decision?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your effective control, then, over the activities of the local banks?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: This is not a decision made by any bank. Secondly, we have to go back to the years 1992, 1993, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and see what could be done and how much could be done. My comment, if you wish, would be as follows: Such decrees, you will find in all the encircled areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tuzla, Bihac, Zenica, and so on and so forth. And you will find the same documents where fines are prescribed in German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of those decisions revoked by you? I mean not by you, by the bank, but by the authorised organs?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: This was not under the scope of authority of the central bank. These are the laws of fiscal nature and the central bank deals only with the monetary part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you report such kind of proposal to the appropriate authorities?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: There was no communication, there were no communications with Sarajevo. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no communication with some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but what about Herceg-Bosna? Did you have any communications with Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: There were no communications between Sarajevo and any other part of -- so there were no satellite, fax, connections, and all the districts, starting with Bihac, Tuzla, Zenica, Gorazde, Central Bosnia, Herzegovina, tried under the given conditions to keep their payment transactions functioning in any possible way. Obviously every area did it in the most efficient possible way, and in the cheapest possible way at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did any local banks inform you of the situation with Croatian dinar and other foreign currency? And the decisions made by the local authorities imposing the use of foreign currency?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: The banks did not look after that. It was not their authority. Again, I repeat, this is the area of fiscal policy. This is not the monetary policy. When it comes to prescribing a provisions regarding fines and payments, and I repeat, every encircled district at the time passed their own local decrees, and fines were prescribed in the currency that was available, which means the cash available. As far as the non-cash transactions are concerned, nothing was being done because there was no economy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's quite clear that the situation was quite difficult, but -- but if the fines are paid through the banks and they were paid through the banks, your authorised banks were supposed to know about the situation with the currency, am I right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: You're not right. Fines were paid by SDK and that was paid in cash or usually in the courtroom. The payment transactions only partly functioned through SDK, very little was done through the banks. There was no, practically no non-cash payments or non-cash accounts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, that is item G, you claimed that more frequently payment operations were performed in stable currency, and you indicate U.S. Dollar, German marks, Swiss francs and Croatian dinars. Do you mean that Croatian dinar was also a stable currency at that time?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: This is not what I considered, but it was a fact that it was a stable currency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean that Croatian dinar was stable currency in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: It was relatively stable because it was tied to the German mark and the rate of exchange oscillated very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it convertible?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: The notion of convertibility requires a broader discussion. Every currency is convertible if somebody wants to take it. The notion of convertibility is no longer -- has no longer its classical meaning, so it's very difficult to talk about the notion of a currency being convertible today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like professor to be shown Exhibit 933.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to facilitate our job here, I just -- attached a covering page to some documents taken from the official Vjesnik on the exchange rate of foreign currency in the Republic of Croatia. Professor, I would like you to take a look at the current list and if you wish, you can look through the Vjesnik. Professor, you just told the Trial Chamber that the Croatian dinar was relatively stable. Please, take a look. For example, at January, 1992, when the rate was 55 Croat dinars for one deutschmark. And now, please take a look at November, 1992. The rate of the Croatian dinar went down sixfold, am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I would like to apologise about our last misunderstanding. It was entirely my fault because I was looking at the left-hand side column of the -- of another decree, and you finally realised that. And I apologise. What I want to say now is that in the Croatian version we can't see it too well but as I -- as far as I can tell, this is 100 German marks, the unit is 100 German marks and here it says 5546, and that's the rate of exchange. I don't know who did this Exhibit 5933, whether it was a financial expert, but this does not reflect the ratio in the rate of exchange found in the Vjesnik newspaper offered by the Prosecution. One thing has nothing to do with the other. It doesn't say anywhere that one German mark is 55 dinars, because it was always calculated on the basis of 100 German marks, not one, and you will see it in -- that the same is true of schillings, American dollars, there is 1.000 schillings and one American dollar and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, the witness is an expert in this aspect. I believe he can tell us what it is. 12

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Croatian dinar was not a stable currency at that time?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the year 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we are talking about 1992 and 1993. In the period when you were the head of the national bank.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, am I right to say that the Croatian dinar was a sort of collapsing currency at that time?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to foreign currencies, but when it came to purchasing power in Croatia, it was not collapsing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was correct that it was beset by the hyperinflation? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to foreign currencies but inflation is measured with regard to the purchasing power of a domestic currency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you think the Herceg-Bosna leadership did not introduce deutschmarks as a foreign currency for circulation in that territory?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: It probably had some cash available to them, cash dinars, and at the time, all the trade towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only Herceg-Bosna but the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, went through Croatia and it was most advisable, and if you wish, most economically justified, to use that foreign currency which figured to the highest level in economic trade. That was economically justified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it economically justified?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Simply, the biggest trade is with a certain state, and it is normal, rather than to convert one currency into another, the payment could have been executed in that one particular foreign currency, and this is often done even in peace time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it wiser to introduce the deutschmark as a convertible hard currency, from the economic point of view?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Then it would have simply been necessary to have enough cash in German marks available. In practical terms it would have meant that the commodity, the it goods that was imported from Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina, one would have had to buy German -- Croatian dinars with German marks and pay for those goods, and I don't think that it would have been justified to introduce some other money, but the money that is used in the country with which there is a highest level of trade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know pretty well that Herceg-Bosna was not isolated. I repeat. And it was easy, it was easy to introduce the deutschmark, right?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No. I explain once again. It is normal and economically justified to use the money used in the country from which most of your imports come, because you don't have to convert three times in order to pay for the goods, and the imports were not only for Herceg-Bosna but for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, for Tuzla, Bihac, because that was the only way one could obtain any sort of goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying that the Croatian dinar could be printed in Croatia and shipped to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No. This is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But where was it printed?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in Germany, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, would it be correct to say that this decision to take the national financial system, to unconvertible, weak foreign currency, cannot be motivated by any pragmatic concerns rather than by political reasons?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: The reasons were pragmatic and economic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question: That's about your position as a governor. You just explained to the Trial Chamber that in April, your report was approved by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all of a sudden, in October, 1993, you were removed from this position.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain a little more, maybe in more details, why did they take this decision in respect of you? In your understanding, of course.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, okay. [Interpretation] I believe that I'm going to give you the facts, not the way I understand them. Firstly, my removal was against the law, and it was not as the result of me not doing my job. I worked as hard as I could under the given circumstances. Secondly, I was the last Croat in the organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who did not want to abandon his post in Sarajevo, and the only solution was to dismiss me, to remove me. Obviously, I continued working as a full time professor in Sarajevo, and at the moment when I could physically go back to Zenica, I continued working as a professor in Zenica. I travelled via Tarcin Kresevo to Zenica, and it is my conclusion that, as far as my work was concerned, there were no reason to remove me from my office of the governor of the central bank. I repeat I was removed because I did not want to leave of my own will from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, is it correct that at some point you worked as president of the management board of the federation privatisation programme? Correct?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the first president of the management board of the federal privatisation agency. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, professor, that in May, 2000, you were removed from this position by the office of the High Representative?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: The reasons were -- let me be brief, and I could give you the open letter that I addressed to Mr. Petritsch after my removal and there you will find the complete explanation, and in one sentence, in a nutshell, if you want to hear that, the reasons would be as follows: I was never a "yes man" when it came to the discharge of my duties, and since I could not take orders, the orders issued by the High Representative, to carry out privatisation beyond the norms and laws, I was removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were supposed to take orders issued by the High Representative.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. The orders which fall beyond the scope of the law did not exist, but verbally, I was asked to break the law, and written orders were always carried out, and I often, in my conversations with the Office of the High Representative, I asked for written confirmation of their verbal requests, and then that these written orders would be carried out. I would have never accepted or carried out any written order if it meant breaking the law. It is not logical that a person who drafted the privatisation project and with his team drafted laws pertaining to the area of privatisation as the president of the management board of the privatisation agency, would prevent the execution of his professional project. You have to admit that it doesn't make too much sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gave you verbal orders?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Representatives of the OHR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their names or positions?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I don't think names are important. Whatever was done at the OHR, one should hold accountable the front men of the OHR. When I was the dean of my department I was accountable to my faculty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 932. Unfortunately, this document is only in the English language but there are only two sentences that are of interest. Maybe the interpreters will help us. I mean that part of the document which deals with reasons for removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. Your Honours, I think it would be fair and in line with your effort to treat the witness fairly to have this document translated in total, as a whole, if the interpreters could interpret it for the witness, the whole text of the reasons for removal, so that the witness knows what it is all about, unless the witness's English is proficient. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am listening and that will be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the witness is familiar with this decision. We have to give the opportunity to this witness and ask him to explain that. Yes. You may have the floor, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the interpreters in the booth to interpret the article that is to give a translation of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor? Which article you would like to draw the witness's attention to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: First of all the decision itself, that's page 1 of the document, and maybe the rest of the text. It's not too much. It means the information will be complete then, and it would be fair to the witness, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you may read the decisions yourself and ask the interpreters to translate it into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right. “Decision: To remove Mr. Stiepo Andrijic from his position of President of the Management Board of the Federation Privatisation Agency. This Decision has immediate effect. Reasons for removal: Mr. Stiepo Andrijic has persistently and seriously obstructed in numerous cases the process of privatisation in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in his capacity as the President of the Management Board of the Federation Privatisation Agency. In particular, Mr. Stiepo Andrijic is responsible for: delaying the adoption of international-standard tender regulations urgently required for the implementation of transparent tenders. The non-adoption of the regulations led to unsatisfactory tender results and an obvious lack of transparency. Insisting, against the advice of domestic and international privatisation experts, on the adoption of an arbitrary and unnecessary deadline of 29th February 2000 for the publication of all tenders. This date led to enterprises being tendered without any acceptable degree of preparation, and under the existing flawed regulations. These two points subsequently resulted in the necessity of the Government, for the Government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to announce suspension of the tender process. Disregarding the strong advice of the Office of the High Representative to implement the recommendations of the Privatisation Monitoring Commission. Compliance with those recommendations would have led inter alia to large hotels being sold under large-scale privatisation regulations and to more satisfactory results. Preventing implementation of the Federation Government's agreements with International Community. Such agreements include that majority undertaking in specified strategic enterprises be offered to strategic investors. Mr. Andrijic's announcement of 10 May 2000 contravened this agreement. Wolfgang Petritsch, High Representative.”

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, do you mean that they were giving you verbal orders relevant to the implementation of the privatisation programme? Was it Mr. Petritsch or someone else who gave you such kind of orders?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I will send to the Court my open letter addressed to Mr. Petritsch commenting on all the elements contained in this decision. However, it is in order to provide a brief preparation for this Court regarding this decision. To begin with, this decision, the President of the management board of the privatisation agency is removed. The management board decides in this agency with nine votes and we have nine members. Therefore, the President could not do anything that would be against the will of those eight votes. What does it mean, that only the President is removed and other members remain, stay on? My vote does not carry more weight than any other votes, and all decisions are passed by the management board. No decision could be taken outside the management board. Secondly, this is a basic issue. I have already explained that it does not make sense, and I apologise for a word that I will use, it is even -- it would be crazy, it would be foolish for a professor, who considers the privatisation process the work of his lifetime, in a manner of speaking, that he himself would be obstructing the implementation of his project. All these allegations are incorrect and in breach of law. The deadline of the 29th is indicated but that is the deadline indicated in regulations. It was not just invented. It also mentions big hotels and so on and so forth. The hotels were privatised in compliance with the law. It is also mentioned that the government took a decision, and it had to change it. In our privatisation legislation, there is not -- the word government is not mentioned a single time, under our privatisation law, the government has no powers at all which is only logical because you cannot have a government which may only be in government two or three months and if cannot decide on property which was created by generations. Therefore, to mention the government in -- within the framework, within the context of privatisation is not nice and is definitely not correct, because let me be brief, this removal took place because when what little property, what miserable property remained in the federation, it was not allowed that the -- that its owners become the citizens of the federation. And when we would not allow that they be bypassed and decided to act in compliance with the law, then they decided to find somebody who would be guilty and that guilty person was the one who would not allow that the law be breached. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but you did not answer my question. My question was a brief one. Who gave you verbal, and you think unlawful, orders? And what kind of orders? In brief.

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: What is written here is all in violation of law and our regulations on privatisation. It does not matter whether it was Mr. Petritsch's deputy or his clerk. To me they are the OHR. And naturally, all the responsibility rests with Mr. Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, is it correct to say that in this situation, when you were the president of this body, you were giving advantage to the Bosnian Croats and the Croats as a whole in realisation of privatisation projects?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: May I answer in our nice Croatian language? That is not true. I cooperated more with areas, conditionally speaking, that were Muslim because they need add little bit more assistance. The sessions of my management board took place in more than 90 per cent in county seats because we believed that that would also be a help to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were talking about the hotels. Do you know who obtained the hotels, as a result of privatisation?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I guarantee that the privatisation of that unfortunate hotel in Sarajevo, which is called Holiday because that is the hotel, although its name is not mentioned, and it was sold in a public tender. I guarantee that. In compliance with all possible regulations. Later on, after I was removed, there were attempts to vacate that sale. But that was not done because not a single fault could be found with that tender and with the sale of that hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. To begin with you, it's a Holiday Inn, in Sarajevo. And the transcript says only "holiday." However, what I want to say is the following. This is an expert witness. His expert knowledge, his findings may be questioned but you see what the Prosecutor is doing, and there is sniggering here. They are trying to discredit this man as a fact witness. Is it now the time to discredit him as a fact witness and about his expert findings, nothing? He should try to discredit his expert knowledge and his analysis rather than the sale of a hotel, even though I was very happy for the courts to hear what was the reality like in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, and I am very glad that you can hear what kind -- how democracy is violated in a country under the guise of democracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, your last question, I believe, is a little bit out of the scope. You have some explanations on that? You may do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I did it because I wanted to check the credibility of the witness. Once an expert is a credible, he must be a credible person and vice versa. That was the point of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you're approaching the end of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Try to finish your cross-examination, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: My final question, my final question now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Croatian kuna now is still in circulation in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: In what sense are you asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it applied in payment -- in payments?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Only in non-cash payments, that is in foreign currencies, and in cash payments, to make it -- to be very truthful, in Mostar, and Herzegovina, in non-cash payments, the currencies used were the ones that the citizens had in their pockets, so in the former Yugoslavia, even in a non-cash payments, they used German marks or Austrian schillings and so on and so forth, but in non-cash payments only in the convertible mark and other foreign currencies. When I say other foreign currencies, then the Croatian kuna is also a foreign currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: That was my final question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't think I would have any questions but now I have to clear up certain matters. Re-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, do you have the right of appeal against this decision?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean that somebody can take a decision and to forbid you from appealing against it?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's how it is. That same person prescribed the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Well, that same person prescribed the constitution for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? Was it not the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina which promulgated the constitution?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, can that self same man the High Representative, remove other people, discharging other duties, for instance judges and everybody else?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: Sure. And if I may add just one sentence. At this moment I have been deprived of my right of suffrage in the country that I was born in. I have been deprived of my right to elect and be elected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't understand?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please explain?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: I have to right to elect or be elected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who prohibited you?

utterances.speaker: STIEPO ANDRIJIC
utterances.text: This decision.
